title: Blessing the children
hook: hands on a child's head: may you be like Ephraim and Manasseh, or like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shalom Aleichem: the song for the two angels who walk you home. Your line was angels walk you home. Did you hum at the door? Day one hundred one.

Think of the last time someone put a hand on your head. Probably when you were small. A parent checking for a fever, a grandparent at a doorway, a coach after a game. It's one of the oldest gestures there is, and one of the gentlest. On Friday night in many Jewish homes, after the song for the angels and before the wine, the children line up, or wriggle, or pretend they're too old for this. And a parent puts both hands on each child's head and says the same few words people have said for centuries. Today: blessing the children.
screen: `A HAND ON YOUR HEAD.` → `CHILDREN LINE UP, OR WRIGGLE.` → `THE SAME WORDS FOR CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: You've met the words already, back in Genesis. Old Jacob, near the end of his life, blesses his two grandsons, Joseph's sons, and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." So that's what's said over sons. Why these two, and not Abraham or Moses? One answer the tradition gives: Ephraim and Manasseh were the first brothers in Genesis who didn't fight. After Cain and Abel, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers, here are two who got along, even when the younger was put first. Another answer: they grew up in Egypt, far from home, and still stayed who they were. For daughters, the words are: may God make you like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, the four mothers of the people, each with her own hard and brave story. Then, in many homes, comes the blessing the priests gave in the Temple, from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Parents say it with their hands resting on the child's head. Some whisper something personal after, about the week, a test, a friendship. Some bless grown children over the phone. Some grandparents bless grandchildren. It's short. It takes maybe thirty seconds a child. And for many kids, it's one of the things they remember most about Friday nights, long after they leave home: every week, no matter what happened, someone put their hands on my head.
screen: `AS EPHRAIM AND AS MANASSEH.` · `THE FIRST BROTHERS WHO DIDN'T FIGHT.` · `SARAH, REBEKAH, RACHEL, LEAH.` · `THE PRIESTS' BLESSING.` · then, large: `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone you love, aloud or silently. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind: a child, a parent, a partner, a friend. Picture their face. If they were here, picture your hands resting gently on their head. If you pray, you can say the old words for them, the LORD bless thee, and keep thee. If you don't, simply wish them well, clearly, in your own words. Stay with them for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Blessing the children. On Friday night, hands on each child's head: like Ephraim and Manasseh, like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, and the priests' blessing.
Your line: hands on heads. Today, tell one person you love what you hope for them, even in a text, even in one sentence. Day one hundred one.

fork.setup: you're choosing the heroes to name when you bless your son every Friday. the tradition picks two brothers. which two, and why?
options: Jacob and Esau, who made peace in the end.
Ephraim and Manasseh, who never fought.
Moses and Aaron, who led the people.
fork.reveal: Ephraim and Manasseh: one answer is that they were the first brothers in Genesis who didn't fight, even when the younger was put first.

what a scholar hears: Genesis 48:20 says 'by thee shall Israel bless', read as the source of the custom; the priestly blessing is Numbers 6:24–26.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 48:20 and Numbers 6:24–26.
Explanations for Ephraim and Manasseh (brothers who didn't fight; stayed themselves in Egypt) are common homiletic readings, offered as 'one answer'. Confirm.
The daughters' formula (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah) is a later custom, not a biblical verse. Confirm framing.
Order of Friday night rituals (Shalom Aleichem, blessing children, Eshet Chayil, Kiddush) varies by family; the hook places the blessing before the wine.
